note: Every judge saw only the advisory text and the finding text, with opaque ids and an order fixed by a hash unrelated to the arm. Two batches: the first judged the two arms that had finished, and jsonrpc was RE-judged with all three once its competitor arm completed, so no arm is judged in a context the others were not. The superseded two-arm jsonrpc verdicts are not included here; they agreed with the three-arm ones on both arms they covered.

judgements.reason: Same write path and same single Right.EDIT gate the advisory is about, but the mechanism it develops is the `doc.enforceRequiredRights` document flag reached through the unfiltered `doc.` switch in updateDocument. The advisory's escalation is the caller changing the page's access rights (a rights object) so that they obtain script right; flipping the required-rights enforcement flag re-enables or disables an existing author's scripts and does not grant the caller script right. Same area, adjacent security control, different mechanism and consequence.

Describes the hardcoded minor-edit flag and constant comment in saveDocument (line 272) as an audit-trail/visibility weakness. No authorization mechanism, no rights change, no privilege escalation - a different defect that merely shares the file.
Read-modify-write with no version or lock check: a lost-update/concurrency defect. Nothing to do with the missing rights checks that let an EDIT-only user change the page's rights.

Unchecked casts of caller-supplied JSON values producing ClassCastException/NullPointerException - a robustness/availability and error-disclosure defect, not the privilege escalation through rights modification.

Log injection / data retention in the unknown-property warn branch. Different mechanism (unescaped logging) and different consequence (forged log records) from the advisory's edit-to-script escalation.

Same class and same save path, and it does claim an edit-to-script escalation, but by a different mechanism: saveDocument sets only the metadata author, so a metadata-only change such as `doc.title` keeps a privileged content author and the injected markup runs with that author's rights. The advisory's mechanism is the caller changing the rights on the page to obtain script right, not stale content-author bookkeeping.

Correctly identifies that the only authorization on the path is checkAccess(Right.EDIT), but the writable control it names is the `doc.enforceRequiredRights` flag in updateDocument. The consequence it derives is re-enabling (or killing) an existing privileged author's scripts, not the caller granting themselves script right by changing the page's rights, which is the advisory's mechanism. Same area and same missing-check theme, different lever and different outcome.
Map.of rejecting a null key/value in updateXObject, i.e. an NPE and inability to clear a cell. A functional/DoS defect, unrelated to the rights-change escalation.
Same unescaped-logging branch as P-016: caller-controlled text written verbatim to the log. Different mechanism and consequence from the advisory's privilege escalation.

Fail-open prefix stripping (Strings.CS.removeStart) in getPropertiesRequiringHTMLConversion, letting the caller force HTML-to-wiki conversion onto arbitrary keys and drop `_syntax`/`_cache` companions. A content-transformation defect; no rights modification and no escalation to script right.
Hardcoded minor-edit flag and fixed revision comment - explicitly claims no exploit path, only reduced history visibility. Different defect from the advisory's missing rights checks.
Optional return-value semantics conflating 'nothing changed' with 'previous value was null' - an API-contract correctness defect with no security mechanism in common with the advisory.
Unchecked casts on request-controlled values causing ClassCastException/NullPointerException. Robustness and error-response defect, not the edit-to-script privilege escalation.
propertyClassReferences documented as optional but dereferenced without a null check - a javadoc/implementation mismatch causing an NPE. Different defect entirely.

This is the advisory's defect: the target XClass in updateXObject/updateAll is named by the caller (classReference plus the per-property propertyClassReferences map), the object is created or overwritten and any property of that class written via xClass.fromMap, and the only authorization decision on the whole chain is checkAccess(Right.EDIT, documentReference) on the document - no allowlist, no comparison against the configured Live Data class, and no check of the rights the named class confers. That is exactly how a user with only edit right reaches the rights-bearing objects on the page and changes the page's rights, which the finding names explicitly as the payoff.

Same fail-open removeStart in the RequiresHTMLConversion list as P-023: caller-chosen names get HTML-converted and companion keys silently dropped. A content-conversion and data-loss defect, not the rights change that yields script right.

Exactly the advisory's mechanism: readBytes() takes the wire-declared 32-bit length, the only guard is `contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE`, and `new byte[(int)contentLength]` allocates ~2 GB before readFully() reads a byte. Same sink (ValueReader.java readBytes), same reachability (readLongstr / field-value 'S' and 'x', pre-auth via connection.start server-properties), same consequence (OutOfMemoryError DoS). Wording about off-path attackers and JVM-wide impact is elaboration, not a different defect.

Different defect: readTable()'s first-wins duplicate-key resolution (`if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(...)`) producing a cross-parser disagreement / header smuggling. Nothing to do with a length-driven allocation; no resource exhaustion, no OOM, different line and different consequence class.

The advisory's defect verbatim: the guard excludes only Integer.MAX_VALUE, so 0x7FFFFFFE passes and a 2147483646-byte array is allocated from five bytes of wire input, before readFully(). Same file/method, same unvalidated length vs. remaining frame bytes, same OutOfMemoryError consequence, same three entry points (readLongstr, tag 'S', tag 'x'). Line cited (86) is inside the advisory's 83-95 range.

Same method and even the same length check, but the opposite branch: it faults the else path throwing UnsupportedOperationException (a RuntimeException) instead of MalformedFrameException. The mechanism is exception-type mismatch in error handling, not attacker-controlled allocation, and the consequence is an unhandled runtime failure on the I/O thread rather than heap exhaustion. Adjacent to the advisory, not the same defect.

Same decoder and the same family of unvalidated wire-declared lengths, but a different sink and mechanism: readTable()/readArray() feed an unbounded length into TruncatedInputStream and terminate the loop on available()==0 rather than on the declared length being consumed. TruncatedInputStream does not allocate the buffer the advisory is about; the finding explicitly treats the advisory's nested allocations as merely one consequence downstream of its broader claim.

Different defect and different file: dependency hygiene in pom.xml (slf4j-api 1.7.36 on an EOL branch, groovy-all 2.4.21 executing at generate-sources). The finding itself states no exploitable path was found. No relation to ValueReader's allocation.

Different defect: readTimestamp() multiplies an attacker-chosen 64-bit value by 1000 with silent long overflow, yielding a wrong Date. Integer overflow affecting application logic (expiry/ordering/replay), not an unchecked allocation, and no memory-exhaustion consequence.

Different defect and different file: an unmeasured end-of-support status for pinned dependencies in pom.xml. It is a coverage/methodology gap about supply chain, granting an attacker nothing by its own account; unrelated to the readBytes allocation mechanism.

Different defect: readTable() returns Collections.emptyMap() for a zero-length table and a mutable HashMap otherwise, so a remote peer picks the return value's mutability and can trigger UnsupportedOperationException in caller code. API contract inconsistency, not a wire-length-driven allocation, and a different consequence.

Different defect: readShortstr() decodes field names with lossy UTF-8 replacement, so distinct byte sequences collapse to one HashMap key and (combined with first-wins duplicates) shadow legitimate keys. A key-collision / smuggling mechanism with no relation to the size of an allocation or to OOM.

Same file and same untrusted-input DoS family, but a different mechanism: unbounded recursion depth in readFieldValue -> readTable/readArray, exhausting the thread stack. The exhausted resource is the call stack rather than the heap, the trigger is nesting depth rather than a declared byte length, and the error is StackOverflowError, not the OOM from `new byte[contentLength]`.

Same as P-031: unbounded nesting in the readFieldValue/readTable/readArray cycle with no depth counter, causing StackOverflowError. Same decoder and same DoS-via-Error-escaping-IOException consequence class, but the defect is missing depth limiting, not the unvalidated length-to-array-allocation in readBytes that the advisory describes.

Describes a correctness trap: the Method constructor writes javaReturnType directly (line 73) so _javaReturnTypeAsClass stays null and getReturnType() returns null, an NPE at a distance. The advisory's mechanism is untrusted class names reaching Class.forName on the JSON path; this finding is about the path that never calls the setter at all, with no attacker input and no class loading.

Exactly the advisory's mechanism: the peer that answers system.describe controls javaReturnType, which the reflective bean fill pushes through setJavaReturnType -> computeReturnTypeAsJavaClass -> Class.forName(String) at line 122 with initialize=true, no allowlist. Same place, same primitive (static-initializer execution and classpath probing), and it also names the follow-on that the resulting Class becomes the deserialization target type via getReturnType().

Same method and same attacker-controlled string, but the defect claimed is log forging/CRLF injection through the IllegalStateException message at line 125, and it states explicitly that no code execution follows from that line. Same area as the advisory's sink, different mechanism (unneutralized concatenation into a log surface) and different consequence (log integrity, not class loading).

The advisory's defect: constructor at 48-49 hands the untrusted map to JSONUtil.tryFill, the public setter eagerly calls computeReturnTypeAsJavaClass, and line 122's one-arg Class.forName loads AND initializes an attacker-named class with no allowlist. Same sink, same trust boundary, same consequence (attacker-selected static initializer, plus a classpath-existence oracle).

Missing defensive copy: getParams()/internal_getParams() return the live ParameterDescription[] (lines 131/140), giving a TOCTOU gap for in-process holders. Different method, different mechanism (mutable-state escape needing code already in the JVM), no relation to the Class.forName class-loading path.

Traces the advisory's exact chain - ProcedureDescription(Map) line 48 -> JSONUtil.tryFill line 49 -> setJavaReturnType side effect lines 92-95 -> Class.forName(javaReturnType) line 122 - and names the one-arg form's initialize=true, the absence of any allowlist/package restriction/three-arg form, and the resulting execution of attacker-chosen static initializers in the consumer's JVM.

Encapsulation/hardening finding: four getters hand out live internal state (params array, the reflected Method, the Class handle). It touches getReturnType() only as an object-exposure concern and requires code already running in the JVM. Different mechanism and different consequence from untrusted-name-driven class loading.

Same code path (eager resolution inside the setter, line 124's catch around Class.forName) but the defect asserted is error handling and timing: only ClassNotFoundException is caught, so version skew or an Error propagates out of a reflectively invoked setter and aborts the parse. Consequence is availability/robustness, not attacker-selected class loading - it even cites the class-loading behavior as a separate finding.

Unchecked cast and dereference of pm.get("params") at lines 52-53 yielding NPE/ClassCastException out of a public constructor. Different field, different mechanism (missing null/type validation), different consequence (unchecked parse failure). Nothing to do with Class.forName.

Same defect as P-001: the Method-based constructor bypasses setJavaReturnType so the derived _javaReturnTypeAsClass is null and getReturnType() returns null. A construction-path inconsistency with an NPE/wrong-type consequence, not the untrusted-input class-loading sink the advisory is about.

Missing validation of the 'params' member (line 53) causing NPE/ClassCastException and a cheap remote parse abort. It is on the same untrusted document, but the mechanism is unvalidated cast/dereference and the consequence is denial of the RPC facility - a different defect from unvalidated Class.forName.

Again the params cast/dereference at lines 52-53 with no null or instanceof check, rated as an unchecked-exception escape / low-grade availability nuisance. Different sink and different consequence from the advisory's class-loading primitive.

A different attacker-settable bean property: the idempotent flag (setter at 171-173) reachable through the same reflective fill, with an HTTP GET / CSRF / URL-logging consequence. Shares only the ingress; the sink, the field and the impact are all different from Class.forName at line 122.

Sits on the advisory's sink but asserts a different defect: the catch at line 124 covers only ClassNotFoundException, so NoClassDefFoundError/ExceptionInInitializerError and a Class.forName(null) NPE escape past a caller's catch(Exception) and abort the parsing thread. Mechanism is exception containment and the consequence is a remote abort; it treats the code-selection primitive as background rather than as its own claim.

Same constructor line 49, but the defect is `this` escaping to external code before construction completes in a non-final class - unsafe publication and a half-initialized object. It reaches the advisory's subject only as one part of a broader claim (that a subclass override of the setter, the natural allowlist mitigation, silently fails), rather than asserting the unvalidated Class.forName itself.

The idempotent flag again (line 171): an untrusted document setting a transport/caching decision documented as authorizing HTTP GET. Different property, different sink, different consequence; it explicitly states no consumer of isIdempotent() was found. Not the class-loading defect.

params is never populated on the no-arg construction path, so getParams()/internal_getParams() can return null while arity() guards it - an inconsistent-accessor NPE. Purely a local correctness defect with no untrusted-input path and no class loading.

Describes the advisory's chain and consequence: JSONUtil.tryFill at line 49 drives the setter to line 94 and thence line 122's Class.forName, so the attacker-chosen class is loaded and initialized before the constructor performs any structural check. Same place, same mechanism (untrusted javaReturnType reaching Class.forName with nothing validating it) and same consequence (the code-selection primitive), framed from the ingress: it is the advisory's 'without any validation' stated as an ordering fact.
